☆ Monotone Local Search with Sample-Dependent Running Times
Serge Gaspers
Monotone Local Search turns an algorithm that extends a given partial solution into an algorithm that finds a solution from scratch: sample a few elements, hope that they lie in an unknown solution, and complete them. Its known analyses bound every call of the extension algorithm by a worst-case time that depends only on the number of sampled elements, and Esmer et al. (SODA 2024) showed that no algorithm that uses the extension algorithm as a black box with this running time beats the original form by more than a polynomial factor. We let this running time depend on the actual sample. If the extension algorithm decides in time $O^*(2^{g(I,X,k)})$, for a polynomial-time computable $g$, whether a sample $X$ can be completed to a solution with at most $k$ elements, our main theorem gives a randomized algorithm with one-sided error in time $O^*(2^{ψn})$ whenever, for some solution $S$ of size $k$ and some $t$, the exponential moment $\sum_{X\subseteq S,|X|=t}2^{-g(I,X,k)}$ is at least $2^{-ψn}\binom{n}{t}$. A corollary, multivariate Monotone Local Search, generalizes the theorems of Fomin et al. (STOC 2016, J. ACM 2019) and of Gaspers and Lee (ICALP 2017). For Max Leaf Spanning Tree and, equivalently, Connected Dominating Set, the previous best polynomial-space bound is $O^*(1.8619^n)$. Completing a sample is a Steiner tree problem, solved in time exponential in the number of terminals, which varies strongly with the sample. We obtain a randomized polynomial-space algorithm in time $O(1.6991^n)$ and a deterministic one in time $(\sqrt5-\frac12)^n 2^{o(n)}=O(1.7361^n)$. For connectivity problems in which the extension algorithm's running time doubles with every component of the sample, an analysis through a partition function gives randomized polynomial-space algorithms in time $O^*(1.8^n)$ for Connected Feedback Vertex Set and $O(1.6444^n)$ for Connected Vertex Cover.

☆ Fresh-Priority Eviction for Cuckoo Filters: Exploiting Latent Randomness Under XOR Hashing
Min Liu
Cuckoo filters are a widely adopted approximate membership query (AMQ) data structure that supports insertions, lookups, and deletions with low memory overhead. At high load factors, however, insertion performance degrades sharply due to the random-walk eviction process, which may require a large number of element relocations. Recent work on bucketized cuckoo hash tables has shown that \emph{fresh-priority eviction}, which preferentially evicts elements whose alternate bucket location has not yet been used, achieves $O(\ell m)$ total expected evictions for bucket size~$\ell$, an improvement over the standard random walk. In this paper, we show that this technique transfers to \emph{cuckoo filters} despite their use of XOR-based partial-key hashing. The key insight is that a fresh element's fingerprint, although stored in the table, is not examined by the eviction policy, so when the fingerprint length satisfies $k = Ω(\log m)$, the alternate bucket hash remains a near-uniform random variable, a property we call \emph{latent randomness}. We prove that under this condition the corruption graph remains subcritical and the total number of evictions is $O(\ell m \log m)$; we conjecture the tighter $O(\ell m)$ bound holds via the full amortized analysis of Bell and Kuszmaul. We further propose encoding the fresh/kicked state implicitly by the element's position within its bucket, requiring no additional per-element metadata. Experimental results on a filter with $2^{22}$ slots and $8$-bit fingerprints demonstrate $1.2\times$ to $2.4\times$ fewer evictions at load factors between $94\%$ and $99\%$ for bucket size $\ell = 8$, and a $1.73\times$ reduction in cumulative evictions to full capacity.
☆ Smoothed analysis of stability radii for the assignment problem
Michael P. Friedlander
Every linear program can tolerate small changes to its costs and still yield a solution of the original problem. The size of this tolerance measures how robust an optimal decision is to noise or numerical error, and how much regularization the problem can support. Classical sensitivity analysis can determine this tolerance only from an optimal solution. This paper provides a priori lower bounds on two measures of this tolerance -- the optimality gap and the $\infty$-norm stability radius -- for the $n$-by-$n$ linear assignment problem over the Birkhoff polytope. The bounds derive from a smoothed analysis, which adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation of at least $σ$ in every direction to an arbitrary base cost. At every fixed confidence level, uniformly over the base cost, both quantities are at least of order $σ/(n\sqrt{\log n})$. The radius bound is asymptotically sharp. Under isotropic noise, the worst case occurs when every assignment has equal cost, and in this case, a scaled stability radius converges in distribution to a standard exponential variable.

☆ A logarithm-free subexponential algorithm for minimum quartet inconsistency
Chuang-Chieh Lin
We give a deterministic algorithm for complete, unweighted minimum quartet inconsistency (MQI) with time and space $2^{O(k^{1/4})}+n^{O(1)}$, where $n$ is the number of taxa and~$k$ is the allowed number of quartet disagreements. This removes the logarithmic factor from the exponent of the MQI bound announced in 2009. The algorithm combines low-error anchoring, chromatic coding, and dynamic programming that accounts for disagreements with all input quartets, with a refined count of colorings and merging states. We also record a generic ETH-based lower bound. The optimality of the fourth-root exponent remains open.

In the online Minimum cost Bipartite Perfect Matching with Delays (MBPMD) problem, $m$ requests and $m$ servers arrive over time in a metric space. An online algorithm has to match each request to a server and can postpone a matching decision by paying the delay cost. The objective is to minimize the total distance and delay cost. Azar, Chiplunkar, and Kaplan gave a randomized $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for metric spaces with $n$ points that are known in advance. For deterministic algorithms, however, the best known competitive ratio in general metric spaces was $O(m^{0.59})$, due to Azar and Jacob-Fanani. On the line, Kuo proposed the Virtual Robust Matching (VRM) algorithm and showed that it is $O(\sqrt{m}\log^2 m)$-competitive. We prove that VRM is $O(\log m)$-competitive for the MBPMD problem in any metric space. VRM is deterministic and does not need to know the metric space or $m$ in advance. It is the first deterministic polylogarithmic-competitive algorithm for the MBPMD problem in general metric spaces. Unlike the previous analysis of VRM, our analysis does not rely on a geometric decomposition of the metric space. Instead, it charges the waiting time of requests over time to the edges of a fixed optimal matching. We also extend VRM to the non-bipartite version and prove that the resulting deterministic algorithm is $O(\log m)$-competitive. This improves the $O(\log^5 m)$ bound of Dufay and Wattenhofer and matches a concurrent result of Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang. The proof that VRM is $O(\log m)$-competitive and its non-bipartite extension were found by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) with almost no human input. We used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) to simplify and present the results. See the AI Usage and Methodology section for details. We take full responsibility for this paper.
☆ Deterministic $n^{O(\log n)}$ Graph Isomorphism Algorithm via Inherited Decompositions

We give a deterministic $n^{O(\log n)}$-time algorithm for graph isomorphism. To our knowledge, this is the first proof of such a worst-case bound for general graphs. The algorithm uses the local-certificate and color-refinement steps of Babai's quasipolynomial algorithm, but retains the decomposition of each recursive instance when it solves an auxiliary coloring problem. There are two reasons for retaining this information. First, a local test can make progress without removing many vertices: it can eliminate a layer of permutation symmetry. A logarithmic bound on the total weight of these layers allows tests of constant size. Second, the auxiliary bipartite graphs arising in the symmetry-breaking step can be represented inside the current instance, after retaining a row decomposition when necessary. These recursive calls inherit the progress already made. The analysis gives a recurrence with quadratic logarithmic cost and a fixed power decrease in every fresh recursive call, improving the explicit cubic logarithmic exponent in the analysis of the corrected Luks--Babai algorithm. We present the algorithm through colorings, partitions, and bipartite graphs, and collect the permutation-group ingredients in one appendix. The result extends to string isomorphism and returns one isomorphism and generators for the full automorphism group.

♻ ☆ Frequency Moments Beyond Equality: Streaming Cosine Density Moments

For a stream of nonzero vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$, let $u_i=x_i/\|x_i\|_2$. We define the cosine density of the $i$-th stream element by $D_i:=\sum_{j\in[n]}\langle u_i,u_j\rangle$ and study the density moments $M_p:=\sum_{i\in[n]}D_i^p$ in both the signed- and nonnegative-cosine regimes. These quantities are similarity-aware analogues of classical frequency moments: replacing cosine similarity by equality (that is, $D_i = \sum_{j\in[n]} \mathbf{1}\{u_j = u_i\}$) gives $M_p=F_{p+1}$ and, in particular, $M_{-1}=F_0$, the number of distinct elements. We give one-pass streaming algorithms and lower bounds whose dependence on $d$ is tight up to logarithmic factors for $p=-1$, $p=1$, and even $p \ge 2$ (the latter under signed cosine), and whose exponents differ by less than $1/2$ for odd $p \ge 3$ under nonnegative cosine. Our results thus extend several fundamental statistics from the classical data stream literature to cosine similarity, a widely used measure for comparing vector embeddings in modern AI systems. The main challenge in proving a space lower bound for nonnegative cosine is to eliminate unwanted contributions without relying on pairs of opposite vectors. We address this through a construction that we call \emph{equal-sum moment isolation}: two insertion-only prefixes have the same cardinality and vector sum, and a finite-difference comparison cancels the baseline shared by all their vectors while isolating the desired higher-order signal. This proof framework may be useful for other insertion-only streaming lower bounds, where direct cancellation is not possible.

An approximate distance oracle (ADO) is a compact data structure that answers distance queries within a multiplicative \emph{stretch} $k$. The classical oracle of Thorup and Zwick~[STOC'01, JACM'05] has stretch $k=2\ell-1$ and uses $O(\ell n^{1+1/\ell})$ space, for every integer $\ell\ge1$. This trade-off is optimal for dense graphs under the Erdős girth conjecture. However, for sparse graphs ($m=O(n)$), their lower bound yields nothing beyond $Ω(m)$ space. The main result of this paper is a nearly tight lower bound for pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs in sparse graphs. A pivot-based $1$-hop ADO gives every vertex $\tilde{O}(1)$ pivots and returns as an estimate the length of a walk of the form $u\to p_u \to p_v \to v$, where $p_u$ is a pivot of $u$, $p_v$ is a pivot of $v$, and $p_u\to p_v$ is a stored distance. We observe that all the state-of-the-art ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time are in fact pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs. We prove that every \emph{pivot-based} $1$-hop ADO with \emph{real} stretch $k$ requires $\widetildeΩ(m^{1+2/(k+1)})$ space, under the Erdős girth conjecture for graphs with constant degree. This matches the best known ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time, at every known stretch, up to polylogarithmic factors. In addition, we obtain a tight lower bound for two-hop hopsets and improved lower bounds for general $β$-hop hopsets.

For $k$ sufficiently separated clusters, we obtain simultaneous additive and multiplicative weak coreset guarantees, with optimal worst-case size $Θ_D(k\varepsilon^{-(D-1)/2})$ when both errors equal $\varepsilon$. We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{Ω(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{Θ(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=Θ(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $Ω(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.

We give a deterministic $O(m)$-time algorithm for exact modular subset sum over every modulus $m$. The input gives distinct residues and their multiplicities. The algorithm reports all reachable residues and answers one target query. It returns a witness when the target is reachable. The algorithm uses $O(m)$ auxiliary words on an arithmetic word-RAM. This improves Potępa's deterministic $O(m\log m\,α(m))$-time bound under the same input convention. The running time matches the cost of returning a length-$m$ Boolean array. We represent reachable residues as runs along cycles of repeated addition. Newly reached residues pay for scans of partial runs. Packed cycle flags make rebuilding take linear total time at the original modulus. A theorem on subset sums of distinct units limits the number of adaptive boundary batches to $O(m^{3/4})$. Radix sorting their $O(m)$ total keys also takes $O(m)$ time.

Coflows capture the collective communication requirements of data-parallel applications, and scheduling them well is essential to the performance of modern data centers. We study non-splitting coflow scheduling in a heterogeneous parallel network whose $m$ network cores may be Electronic Packet Switches (EPS), not-all-stop Optical Circuit Switches (OCS), or all-stop OCS, where every flow must be transmitted entirely through a single core. Previous approximation algorithms for this setting have guarantees that grow linearly with the number of cores $m$ or with the maximum flow degree $τ$ of a port, and therefore become weak as data centers deploy more cores. The source of this dependence is the rounding step: rounding each flow to the core holding its largest fractional value can inflate the load of a port by a factor of $m$. We replace this step with an iterative relaxation rounding scheme that handles the input-port and output-port capacity constraints simultaneously. For minimizing the makespan, this yields approximation ratios of $\min\{τ, 3\}$, $2\min\{τ, 3\}$, and $4\min\{τ, 3\}$ for pure EPS, pure not-all-stop OCS, and pure all-stop OCS networks, respectively. For minimizing the total weighted coflow completion time, we obtain approximation ratios of $8\min\{τ, 4\}$, $16\min\{τ, 4\}$, and $32\min\{τ, 4\}$ for the same three architectures. In a hybrid network, the guarantee is governed by the weakest architecture present, so the overall ratios are at most $4\min\{τ,3\}\le 12$ and $32\min\{τ,4\}\le 128$, respectively. Unlike all previous guarantees for non-splitting coflow scheduling in heterogeneous parallel networks, these bounds are absolute constants that do not grow with the number of cores $m$ or with the flow degree $τ$. We also show that the integrality gap of the underlying linear program is at least $2$.

The Minimum $k$-Cut problem asks for a minimum-weight set of edges whose removal leaves an undirected weighted graph with at least $k$ connected components. We consider only $k\ge3$. The fastest previous algorithm for weighted graphs ran in $n^{k-2}(m+n)(\log n)^{O(k^2)}$ randomized time~\cite{LV26}; on dense graphs this is $\widetilde O_k(n^k)$, and for $k=3$ it gives an $\widetilde O(nm)$-time algorithm. We improve the dense-graph exponent from $k$ to $k-1$ and obtain the same exponent deterministically. After aggregating parallel edges in $O(m)$ time, our randomized algorithm runs with high probability in \begin{equation*} k^{O(k^2)}n^{k-1}\log^2n \end{equation*} time, while our deterministic algorithm runs in \begin{equation*} k^{O(k^2)}n^{k-1}\log^{O(1)}n \end{equation*} time. In particular, weighted Minimum $3$-Cut can be solved in $O(n^2\log^2 n)$ randomized time and in $\widetilde O(n^2)$ deterministic time. The algorithms have two main components. First, we give a faster algorithm for weighted Minimum $3$-Cut. After handling optima with a very small side and optima with two light sides, the remaining optimum has a unique structured side. Tree packing reduces its completion to a batched collection of $2$-respecting cut problems. Second, we reduce Minimum $k$-Cut to Minimum $3$-Cut by enumerating a bounded family of light-cut candidates and recursively completing either side of each candidate. If the enumeration produces too many cuts, then we can instead produce an optimum $k$-cut directly. Jaehong Myung, Seungho Eum, Hyunjung Chung, Unsang Park
Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.
☆ AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
Jiacheng Ding, Yanliang Qi, Cong Guo, Peihua Mai
3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.

☆ Extensible Programmatic Specification of Finite Element Methods
Theadora Fields Collin, Oded Stein, Gilbert Bernstein, Saman Amarasinghe
Finite element methods (FEMs) are a powerful and ubiquitous tool for solving engineering problems. Experimenting with different finite elements can improve the quality and efficiency of solutions. In some cases, the wrong (but nonetheless most common) choice of finite element will produce solutions which converge to the wrong answer regardless of mesh resolution. However, in practice, the choice of finite element is not explored due to the complexity of re-deriving and re-implementing finite element methods. Trying a new finite element is challenging because practitioners must manually deduce formulas to use these elements and implement them within a potentially complex system. We address this problem by introducing ElementForge, a finite element system that is parametric over the literate mathematical specification of a finite element in a domain-specific language (DSL). The ElementForge compiler reasons about tensor spaces, tensors, and tensor bases from first principles to derive implementations of finite elements. The ElementForge compiler is able to automatically derive implementations of finite elements previously only derived by hand. Further, ElementForge minimally couples several key mathematical concepts, mainly tensor fields, mesh topologies, sparse tensors, and assembled finite element operators, to produce a complete finite element system that is parametric over the choice of element. Consequently, the elements derived by the compiler can be applied parametrically to new meshes, PDEs, and boundary conditions. We evaluate our system by implementing several simulations with different finite elements, demonstrating that our system can explore tradeoffs in generality, accuracy, speed, and representational complexity. For example, we are able to implement the Morley, Bell, Argyris, and Hermite like elements with less than 50 lines of code and use them all in a single simulation.

☆ When Benign Is Unverified: Label-Signal Mismatch and Abstention-First Triage in Graph-Based Memory Forensics

Machine-learning triage for memory forensics is usually validated on corpora whose benign class is asserted by provenance and never verified. We report a validation study of a graph-based triage pipeline for Windows memory images: Volatility 3 output is compiled into typed heterogeneous graphs and scored by a temperature-scaled GINE classifier and two one-class encoders, fused with rule risk under an abstention gate. On MalVol-25 a transparent rule layer contradicts the benign label on every control (15/15 and 18/18 flagged; at least 11 of 15 paired controls rated HIGH or CRITICAL), and mean injection and command-and-control counts run higher on controls than on infected captures. We call this rule-label discordance label-signal mismatch; it shows the benign class is unverified, not compromised. Leave-one-family-out AUROC over matched pairs is provably three-valued, so a reported mean and standard deviation identify the fold composition. The learned model (0.786 +- 0.311; 9/4/1, scored in-sample by a frozen checkpoint) equals a logistic model over rule-derived attributes (0.786 +- 0.410; 11/0/3) in mean only, and its significance rests on dropping four saturated ties. The fusion path sends 97.7% of snapshots to analyst review, 95.3% with every gate disabled. Two public feature-level corpora show the same defect: on CIC-MalMem-2022 every benign row carries injected regions and one host-population feature reaches AUROC 0.997 under leave-one-family-out validation; on the Sihwail et al. (2021) sample the injection indicator fires on 53% of benign rows. We close with seven reporting artefacts for learned triage on corpora whose ground truth is asserted.

☆ Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
Jiadong Zhang, Xiaosong Ma
Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

Jiarui Guo, Zhi Zhang, Boyu Tan, Zongwei Lv, Haobo Sun, Na He, Ziqing Wang, Xinfei Shi, Wei Zhang, Xi Yang, Haosheng Hu, Wending Bao, Zetao Hu, Dong Cao, Yong Li, Lining Wang, Chengjun Yang, Tianpeng Wang, Huanbing Lu, Yidan Wang, Hengyi Bao, Yaxin Yu, Hanyun Guo, Huidong Zhang, Haiyu Zhou, Zefeng Liu, Weixiang Huang, Ziyi Wang, Chenyi Song, Ruixuan Zhang, Zhengkai Ao, Haocheng Luo, Zhichen Xue, Jialin Zhang, Chi Zhang, Lingjun Zhu, Silu Zhou, Zongyuan Wu, Yinghao Yu, Yi Zheng, Miao Sun, Yuxing Yuan, Juncheng Yin, Guoding Li, Nan Wang, Xiyu Wang, Lin Yang, Zechao Zhang, Jianning Zhang, Bo Cai, Xiaolin Wang, Tao Lan, Tong Yang, Kan Liu, Lu Chen
Large language models and inference techniques evolve rapidly, making model enablement a recurring production task rather than a one-time integration effort. At Alibaba, a shared inference infrastructure must keep pace with new models and serving capabilities while remaining reliable across heterogeneous production environments. To reconcile rapid evolution with production reliability, we present RTP-LLM, an open-source production inference engine developed and deployed at Alibaba. Its architecture separates model-specific execution from shared request processing, state management, and resource coordination. Explicit interfaces localize compatible model changes while allowing models and deployment configurations to reuse common serving mechanisms. RTP-LLM has evolved from an exploratory system into a shared production engine that supports $\sim$100 models and processes hundreds of trillions of tokens per day. We describe how its architecture and production practices accommodate model evolution and contain the impact of failures, and share lessons for building evolvable and reliable inference engines at enterprise scale.
☆ Beyond Source Compatibility: WebAssembly as a Stable ABI for ARINC 653 Applications
Wanja Zaeske, Patrick Siegl, Florian Hartung, Fabian Bauriedl, Nicolaus Bär, Umut Durak
Thirty years ago, ARINC 653 was introduced to provide a vendor-independent platform for software applications in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA). A platform is characterized by a well-defined interface abstracting over implementation details; in the case of ARINC 653 this is an Application Programming Interface (API), defined on the source-code level. However, several aspects of this API - such as the memory layout and partially also the integer bit width of data types - remain implementation dependent, so portability across Operating Systems (OSs) requires recompilation, and often also source code adaptation. Our contribution is three-fold; first, we refine the ARINC 653 header file, eliminating remaining ambiguities. Second, building on WebAssembly (Wasm), we define an OS- and processor-architecture-agnostic Application Binary Interface (ABI) at the object-code level, resolving differences in data layout, endianness, and function-pointer representation between host and guest environments. Third, we demonstrate a Wasm-VM-agnostic shim-library that executes ARINC 653 partitions, compiled to Wasm bytecode and following our ABI, on multiple processor architectures using two independent Wasm runtimes.

☆ BitLLM: Efficient Low-Bit, Conversion-Hiding LLM Decoding on Mobile GPUs
Hangyu Zheng, Zhihao Shu, Kunxiong Zhu, Minghai Qin, Xiaolong Ma, Gagan Agrawal, Wei Niu
The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unlocked remarkable capabilities across various domains. However, deploying LLMs on mobile devices remains challenging because of their high computational and memory requirements. Low-bit quantization (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) can reduce model size while preserving accuracy, but its practical efficacy on mobile GPUs has been limited so far. In this paper, we identify that the performance gap stems primarily from frequent data type conversions between quantized and floating-point values, and dynamic and inefficient memory access patterns caused by the growing Key-Value (KV) cache during autoregressive decoding. We introduce BitLLM, a mobile inference engine that addresses type conversion overhead and suboptimal memory accesses in quantized LLMs. Our approach features an adaptive layout and packing strategy for the KV cache that ensures efficient memory access throughout LLM decoding. This is coupled with an integer-native execution pipeline that defers and overlaps type conversion outside the compute hot path, keeping the critical MatMul stages in the integer domain. Implemented on off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM outperforms leading engines, i.e., LLAMA.CPP, MNN-LLM, LiteRT-LM, and MLC-LLM, achieving average speedups of 1.78$\times$, 1.73$\times$, 1.58$\times$, and 1.47$\times$, respectively, across various models and quantization levels. Under long-context generation, BitLLM reduces average energy consumption (per token) by up to 88.9%.

☆ Elastic Precision: Software-Hardware Co-Design of a Mixed-Precision Architecture for Long-Context LLM Inference
Boyang Chen, Xiao Wu, Haoran Wu, Yiren Zhao
Low-bit quantization reduces the data movement and computation costs of large language model (LLM) inference, but uniform widths can waste precision and degrade model quality. Existing mixed-precision methods do not fully account for how the other input of the current GEMM tile affects output error when selecting one input's width. Using both inputs to guide precision introduces additional estimation and selection overheads on conventional hardware. We propose Coffee, a runtime precision allocation architecture for long-context LLM inference. Under a fixed average bit-width budget, Coffee combines statistics from both current input matrices to estimate output errors at candidate widths and select each subarray's two input widths, allocating more bits where they yield greater estimated error reductions. Its mixed-precision hardware supports the selected widths in data access and computation, while overlapping error estimation and width selection with transfers and computation to limit stalls. The same read path supports attention-guided KV reads during decoding, reducing memory traffic. Coffee achieves lower perplexity and higher average zero-shot accuracy than the evaluated quantization baselines, and higher long-context retrieval recall than PLENA. For long-context decoding, system modeling projects up to $2.55\times$ the throughput and $2.61\times$ the energy efficiency of the reconfigured PLENA baseline, and up to $4.96\times$ and $12.56\times$, respectively, compared with the B200 GPU baseline.

The design achieves a DSP power efficiency of 0.91 GOPS/W/DSP using only 4 DSPs, demonstrating scalable and energy-efficient DL acceleration for sleep staging that can be extended to other wearable applications.

This letter presents a mixed-precision CNN-LSTM accelerator for EEG-based sleep staging. Evaluated across all 62 subjects in the public MASS-SS3 dataset using 31-fold leave-two-subject-out cross-validation, the mixed-precision approach with hybrid quantization maintains 5-class accuracy within 0.15% of the floating-point baseline when optimized for general sleep staging and N3 sensitivity within 0.51% when optimized for deep-sleep detection. The developed techniques are broadly applicable to EEG-based DL workloads.

This coupling is particularly evident in oriented bird's-eye-view (BEV) detection, where global context, multi-scale interactions, and geometric fusion affect both prediction quality and hardware dataflow. Conventional deployment flows first compress a model using aggregate quality or complexity proxies and then map the compressed operations to a fixed accelerator interface. This separation risks removing geometric structures that appear redundant under coarse metrics but are critical for precise localization, while leaving hardware-level efficiencies in the retained geometry unexploited. We present FieldRT, an algorithm-hardware co-design methodology that uses a common analysis of geometric sensitivity and data lifetime to derive both the deployment profile and its spatial realization. We deploy FieldRT with Axis-Fusion Network (AFN), a sub-million-parameter oriented-BEV detector, and construct controlled profiles that vary the capacity and organization of its geometric processing. The experiments show that redundancy is task-dependent rather than uniform across metrics. Dense prediction can improve while real instance detection deteriorates; coarse localization may remain stable while strict-IoU precision degrades. Moreover, transformations that are individually safe can become detrimental when combined. FieldRT translates the retained geometric structure into a parameterized streaming architecture that shares field access and storage across spatial operators. The resulting custom-PL primitives achieve production-scale numerical closure on an AMD Kria KV260 and make otherwise infeasible multi-dilation execution realizable.

Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.
comment: 9 pages
♻ ☆ Specifying Hardware Communication as Programs
Ernest Ng, Nikil V. Shyamsunder, Francis Pham, Adrian Sampson, Kevin Laeufer
To test and debug hardware modules, it is common to write two programs. A driver maps high-level transactions to cycle-level I/O behavior, and a monitor looks at the low-level I/O trace and recovers transactions. Both programs bridge the same abstraction gap between RTL and functional models. Writing them separately risks inconsistency. ProtoLang is a DSL for specifying hardware protocols. The same ProtoLang program can both drive and monitor transactions. Users specify RTL communication protocols as succinct imperative programs. We present a novel reconstructor algorithm that, given a ProtoLang specification and a waveform, automatically infers a transaction-level trace consistent with the waveform. We demonstrate ProtoLang's utility via case studies focusing on the Wishbone and AXI-Stream interconnects, showing that ProtoLang can model complex protocol features such as burst mode. We highlight how our tools can identify protocol violation bugs in real-world implementations.

♻ ☆ Performance Verification of the AmpereOne CPU Core MICRO 2026
Doa'a Al-Otoom, Nicholas Kelly, Aaron Lindsay, Agreen Ahmadi, Ananth Kumar, Anthony Faubert, Benjamin Chaffin, Bret Toll, Eric Wallace, Lucas Crowthers, Mark Charney, Michael Chin, Michael Spradling, Scott Witscher, Sriyash Caculo, Syed Fakhri, Vivek Kothapalli, William Freelove, Mahesh Madhav
As process technology scaling slows, microarchitectural innovation has become the primary driver of performance gains, making pre-silicon Performance Verification (PV) more critical than ever. This paper presents the industrial-scale PV methodology applied across four generations of the AmpereOne custom CPU core, centered on the cycle-accurate correlation of the RTL design against a trace-driven performance model. The methodology integrates data-driven workload curation, a high-frequency daily regression system, and a unified event-stream framework for analysis. We demonstrate this methodology through case studies of the Branch Prediction Unit and L2 Prefetcher, highlighting a hierarchical strategy that first isolates individual units for focused correlation before proceeding to full-core verification. The results demonstrate that this disciplined, iterative process is indispensable for avoiding costly post-silicon bugs and ensuring complex processors meet their performance targets. We end with a look towards the future of PV in the microprocessor industry.
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures, Presented at the 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO 2026), Athens, Greece
♻ ☆ FAPO: Fanout-Aware Post-Mapping Optimization for LUT-Based FPGAs
Xiaoyu Hao, Keren Zhu
Reducing logic depth during FPGA technology mapping can leave fanout bottlenecks in the resulting LUT network. LUT replication redistributes these loads but consumes area and increases loading on shared fanins. We propose FAPO, a mapper-independent post-mapping optimizer that jointly refines sink assignments and LUT cuts under a final-area constraint. It evaluates replication, cut switching, and recovery by the resulting live LUT count and full-network timing. A necessary all-critical-path condition motivates minimum-cut proposals that complement greedy refinement. Within a fixed critical graph and a restricted same-cut action family, each proposal minimizes the number of copy actions needed to cover all current critical paths. Experiments on EPFL benchmarks show that FAPO reduces the geometric-mean fanout-aware area-timing product (ATP) by up to 14.48% with only a small increase in area. VPR evaluation gives a 6.82% geometric-mean routed-delay reduction relative to ABC if.
Programming Languages 6
☆ WFDB-x: Conformance-Tested Implementations of the WFDB Software Package in Seven Programming Languages
Reza Sameni
The WFDB format is widely used to store and exchange physiological waveforms and annotations. However, existing software implementations are limited to C, Python, and MATLAB/Octave, can produce different results in corner cases and checksum calculations, and have defaults such as sampling frequency and gain, that can lead to silent misinterpretation of recordings. We developed WFDB-x, a cross-language, performance-optimized reimplementation of WFDB in seven programming languages, with extensive unit tests, to provide consistent WFDB processing across programming languages. We reimplemented the WFDB Software Package 10.7.0 natively in Python, C++, Rust, Julia, R, MATLAB/Octave, and Kotlin, using AI-assistance under human direction and review. Each implementation has library functions, a high-level interface, and command-line tools. We compared their outputs with those of the original C programs using 1098 conformance cases, 877 legacy-mode cases, unit tests, and differential fuzzing. Deliberate changes remove implicit waveform parameters, restrict file and network access, and prevent annotation loss. A legacy mode retains the original behavior. All seven implementations passed every conformance and legacy-mode case on the tested Linux platform, with matching outputs. The unit tests contain 9353 assertions. C++, Rust, and Julia read records 1.5-6.9 times faster than the original C library, while the Python implementation wrote records 9.2 times faster than the existing wfdb-python library in the benchmark. WFDB-x provides a tested, open-source basis for reading and writing physiological recordings consistently across seven languages, supporting reproducible research and software development without requiring a shared programming environment. We also share details of the AI-assisted development process and token utilization, which may be useful for other applications.
☆ Stochastic Summaries: Characterizing Structured Datasets Using Probabilistic Programs
Jack Stanek, Adithya Murali
What does my data look like? We study the problem of representing and learning summaries of datasets that account for both their structural and statistical properties. This problem is widely useful across many application domains that involve large datasets and analysis/modeling of data, and is of particular interest to Programming Languages. In particular, in this work we focus on the problem of learning these "stochastic summaries" for tree-like data composed of inductive datatypes and argue that probabilistic programs over inductive datatypes can effectively represent the desired summaries. We present Tali, a Probabilistic Programming Language over inductive datatypes, and study the problem of learning such programs from data samples. We identify a semantic property, called Observation-Bounded Compilability, which identifies a set of recursive probabilistic programs which admit exact inference, and can represent many useful and complex probabilistic structures. We then propose an algorithm for learning Tali programs satisfying the OBC property from observations using a combination of program synthesis (stochastic search) and maximum likelihood inference. We implement our learning framework, evaluate it on a diverse benchmark suite, and record our observations on the merits of our approach. We demonstrate the utility of learning stochastic summaries as symbolically-represented priors for downstream learning tasks. We also showcase another utility by using our technique to learn operational profiles of real-world datasets.
☆ Cartesian closedness of lax comma categories
Maria Manuel Clementino, Fernando Lucatelli Nunes
For a finitely complete category X, we prove that the lax comma category Cat//X is cartesian closed if and only if its free coproduct completion Fam(X) is cartesian closed. The proof uses a change-of-base theorem: postcomposition with a functor induces a left adjoint between lax comma categories precisely when that functor is a left multiadjoint. We describe the exponentials and derive examples from known results on family categories.

☆ XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
Ignacio Cano, Amir Saadat, Rishipal Singh Bhatia, Samuel Ginzburg, Patrick C. Toulme, Ioannis Zarkadas, Praveen Narayanan, Pratik Bhatu, Nicolas Basile, Alexander Dietmüller, Ruishan Wang, Jacob Wahlgren, Victor Barros, Subhankar Shah, Michael Kuperstein, Farzin Houshmand, Emma Sevastian, Peter Gavin, Karthik Srinivasa Murthy, Berkin Ilbeyi, Amit Sabne, Eli Bendersky
Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.
☆ te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
Van Chan Ngo
Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.
