Data Structures and Algorithms 25
☆ Metric Testing: A Characterization of One-Sided Testability
Zihan Tan, Theo Teske
We give a unified framework for one-sided testability (constant-query testing) of metric families. For a broad class of families defined by fixed local predicates, we prove that testability is equivalent to two structural properties: \emph{packing amplification}, which turns many edge-disjoint local violations into a positive density of violations, and \emph{completion stability}, which allows locally consistent partial matrices with few missing entries to be cheaply completed. This characterization yields a common proof strategy and simpler proofs of classical testability results for ultrametrics, tree pseudometrics, Euclidean pseudometrics in fixed dimension, and several others. Our framework also gives new quantitative bounds for metric testing: a nonadaptive one-sided upper bound for matrices with entries in the bounded range $[1,C]$, and two-sided nonadaptive and adaptive lower bounds for general metrics.
☆ A Decomposition Theorem and a Simple Algorithm for Contraction Fixed Points
Xi Chen, Yuhao Li, Mihalis Yannakakis
We prove a decomposition theorem for the problem of computing an approximate fixed point of a contraction map $f\colon [0,1]^k \to [0,1]^k$ under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm. After a preliminary version of the decomposition theorem appeared on arXiv [CLY26], Feodorov and Haslebacher [FH26] gave a striking application of the theorem, showing that it can be used to convert any $\operatorname{poly}(k,\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$ into an algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{k})}$. They instantiated this framework with an $O(k^2\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with the desired running time, thereby obtaining the first subexponential-time algorithm for contraction fixed points under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm and, via well-known reductions, the first deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for simple stochastic games and mean-payoff games. In addition to the decomposition theorem, as our second main result in this paper, we show that the $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm of [CLY25] can be implemented in time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$; our algorithm may be viewed as conceptually simpler compared to the algorithm of [FH26]. A key observation here is that the function constructed in [CLY25], whose fixed points are used as the next query points, turns out to be nonexpansive under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm, so the brute-force procedure can be replaced by known algorithms for contraction fixed points.
comment: To appear in SOSA 2027. This paper subsumes some of the results in our earlier preprint arXiv:2602.10296. This manuscript is an August 2026 snapshot, predating OpenAI's list of papers and the subsequent developments. The discussion and references have been retained as of that date
☆ Reading between the levels: new tools for the Thorup-Zwick hierarchy and their applications
Shiri Chechik, Gur Lifshitz, Avi Kadria, Liam Roditty
In this paper, we develop three new analytical tools for the Thorup-Zwick hierarchy: the Mixed-Level Growth, Two-Level Growth, and Long-Short Growth lemmas. Using these tools, we obtain improved approximate distance oracles (ADOs), and algorithms for $n$-pairs shortest paths ($n$-PSP), multiple-source shortest paths (MSSP), and $ST$-shortest paths, as well as new hopsets. One of our main results is a $(\frac 65 k+O(1))$-stretch ADO with $\tilde O(mn^{1/k})$ preprocessing time and space (where $\tilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors), and $\tilde O(n^{1/k})$ query time, breaking, for sparse graphs, the $(2k-O(1))$-stretch barrier for ADOs with $\tilde O(n^{1+1/k})$ space and $\tilde O(n^{1/k})$ query time. In unweighted graphs, we also obtain a $(\frac 65 k+O(1),O(k))$-approximate ADO with $\tilde O(n^{1+1/k})$ space and $\tilde O(n^{1/k})$ query time. This also yields a $(\frac 65 k+O(1))$-approximation algorithm for $m$-pairs shortest paths ($m$-PSP) in $\tilde O(mn^{1/k})$ time, answering the question of Chechik, Hoch, and Lifshitz [SODA'25] of whether the $2k-O(1)$ barrier for $n$-PSP in $\tilde O(mn^{1/k})$ time can be broken. For unweighted graphs, we give a new analysis of the existing $\tilde O(mn^{1/k}+n^{1+2/k})$-time $n$-PSP algorithm of [Chechik et al., SODA'25], and show that, without any modification, it is a $(k,k-1)$-approximation, i.e., $d(u,v)\le\hat d(u,v)\le k\cdot d(u,v)+k-1$ for every queried pair. This improves its multiplicative factor from $\frac 43 k+O(1)$ to $k$, and the leading coefficient $k$ is tight for this algorithm. Moreover, for graphs with $m=Ω(n^{1+1/k})$, this answers the question of Dalirrooyfard et al. [FOCS'22] up to the additive $k-1$.
☆ A Numerical Refinement of an Exact Discrete Fourier Transform Bound
Zhihao Yao, Sichao Liu
We refine the numerical bounds in Kartal's instantiation of Sussman's exact discrete Fourier transform construction. For every integer n >= 1, the resulting algorithm computes the length-n transform with work O(n (log n)^(1 - delta)), where delta = 0.0030201659. The bound holds in an exact complex-arithmetic RAM model with a supplied canonical root of unity. This final exponent saving exceeds the earlier certified parameter C_0 = 0.00302016 by 5.9 x 10^(-9). We retain the underlying circuit, tighten rational bounds for sums of powers of its block and target ranks, and increase the fixed tensor power from 7760 to 11640. These bounds establish the inequalities for Sussman's recursion at the intermediate certificate parameter C = 0.00302016595. The gap C - delta absorbs the overhead of recursion and Fourier reduction. The resulting transform theorem is proved in Lean and checked against the reference problem statement.
☆ How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
Yu Cheng, Tianle Jiang
We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $ε$-approximate Nash equilibria ($ε$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + ε$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $ε$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $ε$-NE, with matching instances for every $ε$. For small $ε$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $Θ(\sqrt{dε})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $Θ(hε)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $ε$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.
☆ Fluid Limits and Upper Bounds for Randomized Greedy Matching
Sayan Mukherjee
The Modified Randomized Greedy (MRG) algorithm [Tinhofer (1984), Aronson-Dyer-Frieze-Suen (1995)] is a classical greedy algorithm for finding approximate maximum matchings. MRG repeatedly picks a uniformly random unmatched vertex and matches it to a uniformly random unmatched neighbor, if one exists. Since 1991, the best upper bound on its approximation ratio has been $2/3$, given by the Bomb graphs of [Dyer and Frieze (1991)]. We improve this bound to $0.6569$ on general graphs and $0.6607$ on bipartite graphs. Our constructions consist of copies of small gadgets, with specified vertex classes joined completely. We track each algorithm by counting gadget copies with each possible configuration of remaining vertices. Wormald's differential equation method [Wormald (1995)] shows that these counts, scaled by the size parameter of the construction, converge to a deterministic trajectory known as the \textit{fluid limit}, which is described by ordinary differential equations. This fluid limit approximation holds while the relevant vertex classes have positive density, and so we devise a separate counting argument determines the contribution from the end of the run. Furthermore, we apply our framework to Random Decision Order (RDO), in which vertices are processed in uniformly random order and choose unmatched neighbors according to fixed adversarial preferences. On bipartite graphs, we determine the exact limiting ratio on the Double-Bomb family of [Tang-Wu-Zhang (2020)]. Its minimum is $31/48$, confirming their numerical estimate of about $0.646$.On general graphs, we improve their upper bound of $5/8$, given by the paw graph, to $0.5946$ on a new family. Finally, we give one possible explanation for why $2/3$ seemed to be optimal for MRG in the concluding remarks.
☆ The Movement Complexity of Sorting
Sichen Wang
The complexity of sorting is usually measured by the number of comparisons. This measure ignores the movement of the read heads between comparisons, which is a real cost on many machines. We study this cost on its own. Keys lie on a $d$-dimensional grid, two heads move over the grid and compare the keys beneath them, and the only cost is the total movement of the heads. The algorithm plans its route in $r$ rounds and sees the outcomes of each round only after running it. For every $d$ and $r$ we determine the expected movement needed to sort $n$ keys: it is $n^β$ up to polylogarithmic factors, where $β=1+D^{r-1}/(D^{r}-(D-1)^{r})$ and $D=2d$, falling from $n^{2}$ at $r=1$ to $n^{1+1/(2d)}$ with unlimited rounds. Our algorithm makes every round move about the same amount, and a matching lower bound holds against every algorithm.
comment: 39 pages
☆ The Value of Steiner Hubs in Two-Hop Distance Labeling
Sichen Wang
Two-hop distance labelings were introduced in 2002 by Cohen, Halperin, Kaplan, and Zwick with hubs of two kinds: vertices of the graph, or, in their Steiner variant, arbitrary objects carrying arbitrary real values. On no family is the value of that freedom known. We determine it on $\ell_1$ products of betweenness-free metrics, those with no point between two others, a class containing every Hamming graph. The freedom is worth nothing when the factors have at most three letters, while from four letters on the largest saving is polynomial in the size of the product, attained on products of positively weighted stars. The $d$-dimensional hypercube is the two-letter case, and labeling it takes $(5/2+o(1))^d$ entries even with arbitrary hubs, matching the vertex-hub optimum of Goldberg, Razenshteyn, and Savchenko. Every lower bound here comes from one semidefinite program on a single factor, whose value $Λ$ never exceeds the rate that vertex hubs already achieve on the Hamming graph; where $Λ$ meets that ceiling, the freedom is worth nothing, and the ceiling is met exactly up to three letters.
comment: 33 pages
☆ A smaller kernel for Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion
Dekel Tsur
In the Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion problem, the input consists of an undirected graph $G$ and an integer $k$. The goal is to decide whether there is a set of at most $k$ vertices whose removal from $G$ results in a Ptolemaic graph. In this paper, we give a kernel for Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion with $O(k^5)$ vertices. Our result improves upon the $O(k^6)$ kernel of Agrawal et al. [IPEC 2021].
☆ Shared Randomness and Parallel Rounds in Permutation Sampling
Haoxiang Huang
We study the shared randomness needed to sample a uniform permutation in parallel output rounds. Coordinates committed in the same round are independent conditional on the complete history and the current shared choice. Previous outputs are public; local computation and private randomness are free. We charge each shared choice by the logarithm of its conditional support size and sum these costs along the worst execution path. At every fixed round density $ρ\in(0,1)$, the optimal limiting total-variation error under any $o(n)$ shared budget matches the conditional-marginal optimum, even with arbitrary local kernels and adaptive coordination. A fixed improvement requires linear cost. For exact sampling in $R=Θ(n)$ rounds, the optimum is $nΦ(R/n)+O(\log n)$, where $Φ$ linearly interpolates $Φ(1/q)=\log q$. A protocol attaining this rate uses an initial seed and at most one further binary shared choice. When $\lceil n/2\rceil\le R\le n$, the finite optimum is $\log\binom{2(n-R)}{n-R}$, attained by an initial seed alone. The approximate converse uses an entropy inequality for sparse injections to control overlap with the target. The exact construction reuses randomness retained in a shared label partition after the first-stage outputs are exposed.
☆ Subexponential-Time Exact-One Hitting Set
Shiteng Chen, Tao Jiang, Yijie Zhu
Exact-One Hitting Set is one of Karp's original 21 NP-complete problems: given an explicitly listed family of subsets of an $r$-element ground set, decide whether a subset meets every input set in exactly one element. Combining our reduction with the fixed-width exact-counting theorem of OpenAI (2026), we obtain a deterministic polynomial-space algorithm that computes the exact number of feasible selections in time $2^{O(r\log\log(r+16)/\sqrt{\log(r+16)})}\operatorname{poly}(L+1)=2^{o(r)}\operatorname{poly}(L+1)$, where $L$ is the input length. The number and widths of the input sets are unrestricted. Known row selection retains at most $r+1$ input constraints, but their total width may remain quadratic. Our path representation of two-query counting cancellation constructs two ordinary 3-CNF formulas with at most $2r$ variables and $O(r^2)$ clauses each, whose model counts differ by the desired answer. The auxiliary-variable budget depends on the number of simultaneous conditions, not on their widths or on the numbers of witnesses. We extend this construction to signed equations with fixed bounded demands and positive integer coefficients. We also represent every explicitly listed Boolean relation of VC dimension at most one by binary clauses and signed exact-one equations on its original variables, obtaining the same two-query variable bound for unrestricted overlaps among such local constraints. A bounded-term version further handles fixed finite/cofinite local degree rules on arbitrary graphs. The path representation is related by variable elimination to existing marker--parity cancellation.
comment: 33 pages, full version including proofs and appendices
☆ Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
Jiahe Li, Jerome P. Reiter
The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.
☆ $\ell_{\infty}$ norm SVP in $\widetilde{O}(3^n)$
Yiming Gao
We give a classical randomized algorithm for the Shortest Vector Problem in the infinity norm in $\widetilde O(3^n)$ time and space, improving the previous bound of $2^{2.443n+o(n)}$. We adapt Gaussian difference dynamics to the infinity norm by repeatedly taking differences of vectors from two lists, producing lists in successively smaller cubes. The key is to restrict the midpoint of each pair to a fixed inner cube, so that every allowed difference has the same region of possible midpoints. Using random lattice translates, this rule preserves equal expected counts at each point of the smaller cube. We analyze the dependencies created by repeated differencing through the counting moments of Gaussian difference dynamics, together with a weighted packing bound for cubes. Finally, two searches based on coordinate comparisons generate the intermediate lists and recover a shortest lattice vector within the claimed time bound.
☆ Testing MAX-CUT in the Adjacency Matrix Model: Tight Non-Adaptive Bounds and a Cubic Adaptive Lower Bound
Songhua He
We study the query complexity of approximating the MAX-CUT value to additive error $\varepsilon n^2$ in the adjacency matrix model. This was one of the first problems studied in the area of graph property testing [GGR, JACM'1998]. Previously, the best known upper bound for both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms was $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ [MS, SODA'2008; GMRS, ICALP'2022]. The only known lower bound was a trivial $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ bound. We close this gap from both sides for non-adaptive algorithms, proving that its query complexity is exactly $Θ(1/\varepsilon^4)$. We also prove an adaptive $Ω(1/\varepsilon^3)$ lower bound. Our upper bound is achieved by a canonical tester that samples $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ vertices in expectation and outputs the rescaled MAX-CUT value of the induced subgraph. We prove its correctness by applying spectral truncation to the adjacency matrix, using a geometric argument to control the sampling error of the retained low-rank part and a cut-norm restriction estimate [RV, JACM'2007] for the remainder. As an application, an analogous proof also yields a tight $O(1/\varepsilon^4)$ non-adaptive query upper bound for MAX-2CSP. For our lower bounds, we show indistinguishability between a uniform random graph and a distribution that plants a hidden partition. For the non-adaptive lower bound, we observe that one plus the $χ^2$-divergence between the query transcript distributions is exactly a normalized Ising partition function, which can be bounded using Boolean hypercontractivity. For the adaptive lower bound, we view each query through the algorithm's ability to predict whether its endpoints lie in the same part of the hidden partition. We bound the combined advantage of these predictions using the completed transcript, which lets us analyze the adaptively chosen pairs together despite their dependence on earlier answers.
☆ Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
Matthew Ding, Mark Zhandry
Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = Ω(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=Ω(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.
comment: 34 pages
☆ Facility Location with Customer Incompatibilities
Zachary Friggstad, Pengfei Wu
We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities. Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments. It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.
☆ Limits and Constants of OpenAI's Claimed ETH Refutation
Fabio Dias, Yvens Lima
A recent OpenAI preprint claims a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF formula in time $2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, and $2^{O(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ at bounded clause density, which would refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The headline bound is proved by tensor contraction; the body develops an interpolation algorithm with the weaker exponent $n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}$. This note does four things. First, it explains the interpolation algorithm in plain terms. Second, it asks how large $n$ must be for the bounds to bite. The preprint states no constants, so we treat the hidden constant $C$ as a parameter: the general bound beats the $2^n$ of brute force only beyond $n\approx 10^{32}$ for $C=2$, $10^{126}$ for $C=3$ and $10^{3517}$ for $C=10$. We then extract the constants from the tensor-contraction proof: for every input with $m$ clauses at bounded density, the running time it certifies stays above $2^n$ unless $\log_2(n+m)>10^9$, and on random 3-CNF at the satisfiability threshold unless $\log_2 n>5\times10^{11}$. So the bounds are subexponential as $n\to\infty$, but the proof certifies no speed-up over brute force for any input of bounded density that could ever be written down. Third, for the clause-product form of the interpolation algorithm we prove limits in a cost model matching the preprint's evaluation. By a short algebraic lemma, polynomial cost needs components of $O(\log^3 n)$ variables with per-point evaluation, or primal treewidth $O(\log^2 n)$ with dynamic programming over the groups. So the scheme costs $2^{Ω(\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}})}$ at treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $2^{Ω(\sqrt n)}$ with high probability on random 3-CNF above clause density 3, and $2^{Ω(n^{1/3})}$ even on trivially countable path formulas. We explain why the preprint's sharper routes escape these limits. Fourth, we report experiments.
♻ ☆ Extending Tardos's Theorem to Separable Convex Quadratic Programming
Bin Cui, Hanqing Li, Xupeng Miao
For an integer equality matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{r\times m}$ of binary encoding length $\langle A\rangle$, Tardos's theorem solves linear programs using $\operatorname{poly}(r,m,\langle A\rangle)$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, independently of the right-hand side and objective coefficients. We extend this guarantee to continuous separable convex quadratic programming over $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$: the operation count is independent of the right-hand side, linear costs, and all nonnegative quadratic weights. The algorithm returns an exact optimal primal-dual pair or a certificate of infeasibility or unboundedness. All intermediate rational numbers have encoding lengths polynomial in the total input length. As an application, we obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for continuous multicommodity flow with shared capacities and quadratic costs of aggregate arc flow, independently of demands, capacities, and cost coefficients. Objective compression and continuous-integer proximity yield a local solver returning a point close to an optimum. We relax nonnegativity on coordinates with zero optimal dual slack, minimize the largest remaining coordinate, and optimize over the relaxed coordinates. A descent LP over the recession cone provides a complementary bound. Circuit decomposition combines these bounds into a scale ensuring that each local call reveals a new coordinate. At most $m$ calls, followed by two LPs, recover an exact optimum and its dual certificate.
comment: 13 pages, no figures. Substantially revised with a simplified algorithm and proofs. Title and author list updated
♻ ☆ A Simple Randomized Estimator for Harmonic Numbers and Logarithms
Ali Dasdan
Scanning a list of $x$ distinct numbers in uniformly random order for its maximum replaces the running maximum $H_x$ times on average, where $H_x$ is the $x$th harmonic number. Run backwards, this gives an estimator: the replacement count of a random list is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of $H_x$, and since $H_x = \ln x + γ+ O(1/x)$, a corrected estimate of $\ln x$. We give the exact variance of the count, an error decomposition with sample-size rules, and an exact sampler of the count using $H_x$ integer draws on average instead of a scan of length $x$. Coupling two counts estimates $\ln(a/b)$ without $γ$, and a binary range reduction then bounds the standard error by $\sqrt{\ln 2/n}$ for every $x$ at fewer than $1.7$ draws per repetition on average. A classical deterministic series on the same reduction reaches the rounding floor with sixteen terms in the reported experiments, quantifying the gap between the two approaches. The purpose is pedagogical: the analysis of an algorithm becomes an estimator of the quantity that analysis produces, with exact variances, finite-sample error bounds, reproducible experiments, and machine-checked algorithm contracts and moment identities. The ingredients are classical; the contribution is their assembly.
comment: v3: substantially revised and extended third version; title changed from "A Simple Randomized Algorithm to Compute Harmonic Numbers and Logarithms". 22 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code, data, and Dafny proofs at https://github.com/alidasdan/randomized-harmonic-logarithms
♻ ☆ Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
Dimitris Fotakis, Laurent Gourvès, Aris Pagourtzis, Panagiotis Patsilinakos
In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.
♻ ☆ Temporal Conductance and Bounds on the Voter Model for Dynamic Networks
Tatiana Rocha Avila, Holger Dell, John Lapinskas
The voter model is a classical stochastic process that models how opinions might spread through a network: at each step, every node lazily adopts the opinion of a random neighbour; eventually all nodes share the same opinion (consensus). Stronger connectivity should yield faster consensus. Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, and Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016) make this precise via the network's conductance: if the network has $m$ edges, minimum degree $d_{\min}$, and conductance at least $φ$, then the voter model reaches consensus in expected $O(m/(d_{\min}φ))$ steps. Their results extend to dynamic networks with fixed vertex degrees by considering the network's conductance at each time step. We introduce temporal conductance $Φ$, a more general connectivity measure for dynamic networks. Unlike static conductance, which collapses to $0$ whenever some snapshot is disconnected, $Φ$ captures connectivity through edges that appear at different times. We generalise the results of Berenbrink et al. from static conductance to temporal conductance, showing that the expected consensus time of the standard voter model is at most $O(m/(d_{\min}Φ))$. Moreover, we prove that this bound is tight up to constant factors. We expect temporal conductance to be a useful primitive for analysing other dynamics on temporal networks, and potentially time-inhomogeneous Markov chains more generally.
♻ ☆ Tight (Double) Exponential Bounds for Identification Problems: Locating-Dominating Set and Test Cover
Dipayan Chakraborty, Florent Foucaud, Diptapriyo Majumdar, Prafullkumar Tale
We investigate fine-grained algorithmic aspects for classical identification problems in graphs, namely LOCATING-DOMINATING SET, and in set systems, namely TEST COVER. In the first problem, an input is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and an integer $k$, and the objective is to decide whether there is a subset $S$ of $k$ vertices such that any two distinct vertices not in $S$ are dominated by distinct subsets of $S$. In the second problem, an input is a set $U$ of items, a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $U$ called tests, and an integer $k$, and the objective is to select a set $S$ of at most $k$ tests such that any two distinct items are contained in a distinct subset of tests of $S$. For our first result, we show that LOCATING-DOMINATING SET (respectively, TEST COVER) parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph (respectively, the incidence graph) does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$ (respectively, $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$), unless the ETH fails. Next, we prove that, unless the ETH fails, LOCATING-DOMINATING SET does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{o(k^2)} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$, nor a polynomial-time kernelization algorithm that reduces the solution size and outputs a kernel with $2^{o(k)}$ vertices, and TEST COVER does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(k)}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$ nor a kernel with $2^{2^{o(k)}}$ vertices. Again, we show that these lower bounds are tight by designing (kernelization) algorithms with matching running times.
comment: Appeared in proceedings of ISAAC-2024
♻ ☆ Streaming Right Multiplication over Grammar-Compressed Matrices: A Memory-Bounded GPU Engine for Genotype and Graph Data
Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli
Grammar-compressed matrices store a matrix's non-zero structure as a RePair straight-line program (SLP), supporting matrix-vector products in time and space proportional to the compressed size. We target the regime where this is decisive on a GPU: when the uncompressed matrix exceeds device memory, so footprint (not floating-point throughput) is the binding constraint. Our SLP is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of out-degree 2, and the right product $y=Mx$ is a single bottom-up sweep (leaves to roots): a conflict-free gather. We make the grammar properly layered (every nonterminal child one level below its parent) via pass-through completion, which inserts identity nodes to carry values upward until consumed. This yields a streaming evaluation in which each level reads only the level below and writes the next, so the live set fits in two alternating read-only/write-only buffers instead of scaling with the whole grammar. On genotype matrices, where a polygenic score is exactly the right product $y=Gβ$, a CUDA implementation shows a clear space advantage: a device footprint 3.5 to 8 times smaller than a materialized cuSPARSE CSR baseline, single-vector times within a small factor of cuSPARSE, and consistently lower GPU energy. Because the sweep needs only an associative and commutative combine, the same engine evaluates any homomorphism into a commutative monoid over the grammar by swapping a small leaf/combine/emit policy; the same reachability sweep scales to a billion-edge Software Heritage graph (261 TB dense, 21 times smaller serialized than cuSPARSE's CSR). We frame this as an algorithm-engineering case study: structural metrics (depth, live-set width, completion cost) are measured, architecture-independent grammar properties, whereas time and energy are profiled on a single board.

♻ ☆ Tight weighted paging with delay via mirror descent
Julian Born, Yann Disser, Linda Thelen
We give an O(log k)-competitive randomized algorithm for weighted paging with delay. This improves upon the O(log k log n)-competitive algorithm of Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi (STOC 2020, SICOMP 2022) by removing the dependence on the number n of pages. Without delay, the optimal competitive ratio of randomized algorithms is Theta(log k), and since the lower bound carries over, our bound is tight. Our algorithm is fractional and combines mirror descent, used by Bubeck et al. (STOC 2018) for weighted paging without delay, with preemptive service, introduced by Azar et al. (STOC 2017) for online service with delay: when a request is served, an increase in the mirror descent potential is offset by preemptive service to other pending requests, with a budget derived from the mirror descent path. To obtain a randomized algorithm, we use the online rounding of Bansal, Buchbinder, and Naor (FOCS 2007) from classical paging.
♻ ☆ Optimal Labeling Schemes for $Γ$-Free Matrices
Sankardeep Chakraborty, Seungbum Jo
We study labeling schemes for $p \times q$ $Γ$-free binary matrices, which do not contain a submatrix of the form $Γ= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. We give a labeling scheme that uses $O(\log^2 N)$-bit labels for rows and columns, where $N=p+q$, such that any matrix entry can be determined from the corresponding two labels in constant time in the word RAM model. The worst-case label size matches the counting lower bound up to constant factors. We also show that the entrywise least $Γ$-free supermatrix of an arbitrary $p\times q$ binary matrix, together with its labels, can be constructed in $O(pq)$ time. Our construction represents a $Γ$-free matrix by a sequence of rooted forests, where each column corresponds to a node and the $1$-entries of each row form a root path in its corresponding forest. For $n$-vertex strongly chordal and chordal bipartite graphs, our result gives asymptotically optimal $O(\log^2 n)$-bit adjacency labeling schemes with constant-time queries. These results answer both representation questions posed by Spinrad in 1995.

☆ Precision Through Play: Enhancing Fundamental Laparoscopic Skill Acquisition Via Gamified XR and Pseudo-Haptics
Bita koohestani, Ashkan Rezaei, Azam Bastanfard
Extended Reality (XR) technologies have shown potential to improve laparoscopic skills acquisition. Among fundamental skills in laparoscopic surgery is accurate instrument handling. Appropriate instrument alignment and a perpendicular path ensure movement efficiency and improved performance. This work introduces an interactive XR platform designed to support an immersive, engaging, and accessible environment that facilitates continuous practice. This platform incorporates a gamification layer enriched by pseudo-haptics that generate a motivational feedback loop, allowing trainees to continuously practice instrument manipulation and angle control. The platform monitors instrument orientation, computes angular deviation from an ideal reference vector, and assigns scores based on user performance. A point-based scoring component reinforces correct technique and penalizes deviations in tool alignment beyond predefined thresholds. Furthermore, a pseudo-haptic feedback mechanism is integrated to provide real-time tactile feedback when deviation exceeds tolerance. Combined with low-cost hardware and accessible deployment, the framework aims to increase training scalability, engagement, and improve skill acquisition. Preliminary evaluations indicate that integrating gamified feedback significantly improves precision, reduces angular variance, and encourages sustained practice.
☆ Composable CAD: Sketch-to-CAD Program Synthesis in Parts
Yuanbo Li, Vivian Liu, Sean Liu, Justin Matejka
Designers often build CAD models part by part, and may iterate on individual components throughout the design process. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can synthesize CAD programs from sketches, but generating parts independently does not ensure that they are composable: components may lose the intended proportions and alignments or fail to join correctly where they meet. We present Composable CAD, a framework that uses off-the-shelf VLMs to synthesize a design space of independently sampled, interchangeable component programs, where any selection composes into a coherent CAD model. We recover design constraints from the sketch and use them to construct a coarse proxy that establishes how the components are sized, aligned, and attached. We then generate each component independently from its proxy and apply a deterministic rewrite to ensure that neighboring components meet at their prescribed interfaces. We evaluate Composable CAD across a range of objects and sketch styles and conduct two user studies. Compared to VLM-only baselines, our method produces more detailed, composable designs.
☆ SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
Kunal Bhosikar, Prajas Wadekar, Venkata Sai Pranav Bachina, Ankit Gangwal, Charu Sharma, Nicole Meng, Yingjie Lao
4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.

☆ Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
Amin Najafgholizadeh, Mohsen Afsharchi
Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

☆ UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models
Long Vu, Tan Ngo, Animesh Karnewar, Amir Habibian, Binh-Son Hua, Hung Bui, Minh Hoai Nguyen, Phong Nguyen
We present \textbf{UniCaMo}, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead.

☆ Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning
Zixi Yi, Gary P. T. Choi
Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. For topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. Many mapping methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input--output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by $10.17\%$ and $10.97\%$, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. We also apply the framework to other spherical mapping methods including the conformalized mean-curvature flow and spherical density-equalizing maps. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.
♻ ☆ CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-agnostic animation compression with a learned entropy model
Mingyi Shi, Huancheng Lin, Taku Komura
Skeletal motion is stored as every joint's transform at every frame, yet most of it is implied by the body rather than by what the motion is about. Compression is one way to ask what a motion must still say once the body is known, and a production codec must answer it for any skeleton with a stated error bound. Our earlier codec, CurveCodec, matched the mean error of ACL, the production library of modern game engines, with a learned prior over sparse anchors, but not ACL's worst case, and it counted its payload as floats rather than bits. Here we ask where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies and which part of a codec a learned model should take over. Measurements give three answers. At production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each quantized curve from its own past, the second from choosing per joint, in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples not to code. On the gaps such an encoder leaves, a nearest-neighbour oracle over millions of training samples is no better than linear interpolation, and no learned in-betweener we tried paid for itself. What a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals the codec must send. CurveCodec 2 codes every sub-track as a curve in the log map, quantized in closed loop and thinned to rate-distortion-selected keys, with residuals entropy-coded under a small learned model whose integer inference is bit-exact across platforms. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL's own worst case per joint within a stated tolerance, or ACL's mean error per clip. On a held-out test side of 4,472 clips from 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37x ACL's bytes at ACL's default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract and 0.22x at 0.1 cm under the mean contract, decodes on one CPU core, and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training. Project page: https://rubbly.cn/publications/curvecodec/

♻ ☆ DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Mechanics on GPU
Kemeng Huang, Bowen Ren, Xinyu Lu, Minchen Li, Taku komura
Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.
2026-10-30
Operating Systems 1
♻ ☆ Idle Cycles Are Not Wasted Cycles
Matheus Stolet, Simon Peter, Antoine Kaufmann
Idle network service cores are treated as wasted compute. This assumption motivates increasingly sophisticated mechanisms that reclaim idle cores at microsecond timescales. We argue that this view no longer matches modern server hardware. On contemporary multicore processors, active cores compete for a shared package-level power and thermal budget. Once that budget becomes the limiting resource, an idle core that waits efficiently returns compute capacity that hardware can redistribute to productive work. Measurements on a recent AMD EPYC processor show how waiting strategy, processor topology, and idle duration determine this trade-off. Our results suggest that reclaiming idle cores often yields less benefit than commonly assumed while introducing substantial scheduling complexity. We propose a budget-centric view of service-core systems in which power, rather than core occupancy, becomes the fundamental resource and waiting policy becomes a first-class systems design choice.

☆ Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads SC26
Mohsen Zand, Trung Dac Nguyen, H. Birali Runesha
We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. An ML-based surrogate predicts the frequency-dependent complex admittance of individual routes, enabling reuse across matching network topologies and physical layouts for the same technology node without retraining. These route models guide post-layout passive retuning to recover matching performance while preserving the layout footprint. Across nine LC matching networks operating at 5-95GHz, our framework recovers S_11 from -6.37dB, for schematic-level optimization after post-layout degradation to -22.27dB after EM-aware post-layout refinement. All designs meet matching targets under full-layout EM verification in optimization runtimes below 70s.

☆ The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
Guy Lemieux, Michael L. Overton
Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.

However, on-chip memory technology including cell type, bank organization, and process node, is rarely treated as a first-class citizen in DSE. For example, increasing memory capacity can reduce memory accesses through greater data reuse, but at the cost of higher area and access energy, thereby limiting the compute units budget. Consequently, memory technology can fundamentally shift the optimal accelerator architecture for a given area and EDP budget. Existing machine learning (ML)-based DSE methods require repeating simulation, data generation, and model training for each new memory technology. We present TADA, a memory technology-aware DNN accelerator performance and energy estimator that predicts system latency and energy for a given workload, hardware configuration, and memory technology. TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset that generalizes across memory technologies. The dataset spans current and future technology trends while enforcing physics-based guardrails to preserve realistic area-energy trade-offs. Each memory technology is represented by a technology signature, a vector of read energy, write energy, and storage capacity across a range of areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration. Across 21 unseen technology curves spanning SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM, and CTT, TADA predicts system energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error, respectively. In three pairwise case studies, it matches the simulator-selected memory technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets, with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, while achieving over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.

Pipelining the index derivation function (IDF) alone is insufficient: in three of the four variants, other components become the frequency bottleneck, reducing frequency by up to 35% relative to the baseline set-associative cache. Redesigning the critical paths while preserving mappings, rekeying, and victim-selection policies brings the three affected variants to no more than 10% below the baseline frequency, at the cost of added latency or reduced concurrency. Increased LLC access latency, rather than additional misses, dominates IPC degradation, reducing instructions per cycle by up to 5% for SPEC and 11% for GAPBS. Hardware overhead depends on the design and implementation technology: FPGA lookup-table usage increases by 10-35%, while ASIC area increases by 1-14%.

These issues emerge from how circuit stages combine, a structure that generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA do not capture. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. Modern computing architectures, however, are optimized for large-scale arithmetic and struggle with such context-dependent sequential prediction or "cognitive" tasks. ♻ ☆ Idle Cycles Are Not Wasted Cycles
Matheus Stolet, Simon Peter, Antoine Kaufmann
Idle network service cores are treated as wasted compute. This assumption motivates increasingly sophisticated mechanisms that reclaim idle cores at microsecond timescales. We argue that this view no longer matches modern server hardware. On contemporary multicore processors, active cores compete for a shared package-level power and thermal budget. Once that budget becomes the limiting resource, an idle core that waits efficiently returns compute capacity that hardware can redistribute to productive work. Measurements on a recent AMD EPYC processor show how waiting strategy, processor topology, and idle duration determine this trade-off. Our results suggest that reclaiming idle cores often yields less benefit than commonly assumed while introducing substantial scheduling complexity. We propose a budget-centric view of service-core systems in which power, rather than core occupancy, becomes the fundamental resource and waiting policy becomes a first-class systems design choice.

This paper presents Arapai, an offline-first large language model architecture designed for AI-assisted learning in low-connectivity settings. The system performs all inference locally using quantized language models and incorporates hardware-aware model selection to enable deployment on low-specification, CPU-only devices. The system was evaluated with 120 students and 9 instructors from secondary and tertiary institutions under limited-connectivity conditions. We present Generative Logic (GL), a deterministic computer architecture for automated mathematical reasoning. GL starts from axiomatic definitions written in a minimalist Mathematical Programming Language (MPL) and explores a configurable region of their deductive neighborhood. The definitions are compiled into a grid of Logic Blocks (LBs). An LB applies rules by hash-table lookups, and every statement it derives keeps its complete provenance. A run generates conjectures, removes those that counterexamples refute, tries to prove the rest, reduces the proved theorems to an essential core and writes every proof as navigable HTML. An independent verifier checks every proof step. From supplied definitions, GL derives the basic laws of Peano arithmetic and Gauss's summation formula. From previously proved lemmas, further definitions and a supplied list of conjectures, it builds a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA). These proofs are also exported to Lean 4 and checked by the Lean kernel. The next step is for GL to derive the FTA as well, without supplied conjectures. GL is designed together with a hardware architecture, the Mathematical Processing Unit (MPU).

Our main metatheoretic result shows that operational evaluations agree with the denotational semantics under an arbitrary choice of coordinates. ☆ Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic
Bryan Ford
A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence as true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)'s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former $ν$ with Park's coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body's leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every $ν$-body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model wherever it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy replaces the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded by the derivable one that its steps are decided; the change of model pays for the move. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling arithmetic OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu's trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result.

For every fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and independent continuous coordinates, the optimal failure probability is of order $1/[(\log n)^{d-1}\log\log n]$, both with full information and with coordinate ranks alone. A deterministic rank rule attains the optimal leading term uniformly over the marginals. For every fixed positive definite Gaussian covariance, the same failure order holds, with a leading constant depending on the correlation matrix, and a rank-based rule attains the optimal leading failure probability without knowing the Gaussian parameters. In both models, we determine the optimal fixed cutoff and its leading failure constant; its failure probability exceeds the unrestricted optimum by a factor $Θ_d((\log\log n)^2)$. Under arbitrary dependence, a fixed joint density with uniform marginals can instead have optimal full-information success tending to approximately $0.58$. The proof uses the scarcity of observations with very small domination probability to bound every stopping rule. A matching rule selects a currently maximal point when this probability is below a threshold that increases as time runs out. Coordinate ranks from an initial sample provide sufficiently accurate estimates to preserve the optimal leading failure probability. For singular Gaussian distributions with known correlations, we characterize the optimal failure asymptotics attainable using ranks. Singular dependence can make every observation acceptable or recover the difficulty of selecting a single best point.
comment: 48 pages, 8 figures. A preliminary version has been accepted to WINE 2026
☆ Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
Lucas Rosenblatt, R. Teal Witter, Christopher Musco
Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$. In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data. We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/α)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/α^2)$ random directions guarantees $α$ Sliced Wasserstein error. Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.

Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $m$ vertices. After $O(m)$-time preprocessing of $P$, for any set $S$ of $n$ additively weighted point sites, we compute an implicit additively weighted geodesic Voronoi diagram in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time, supporting nearest-neighbor queries in $O(\log(n+m))$ time. In contrast, explicitly constructing the diagram requires $Ω(m)$ time. Our algorithm introduces a new sweep-line paradigm that avoids explicitly constructing the diagram, together with a novel technique for point location in implicit subdivisions. As applications, we obtain new dynamic data structures for additively weighted geodesic nearest-neighbor searching and the first efficient algorithms for shortest paths in geodesic disk graphs. After the same $O(m)$-time preprocessing, single-source shortest paths in a geodesic disk graph of $n$ sites can be computed in $O(n\log n+n\log^2 m)$ time in the unweighted case and $O(n^{3/2}(\log n+\log^2 m))$ time in the weighted case. We also extend our techniques to implicit farthest geodesic Voronoi diagrams for unweighted sites, obtaining analogous bounds and dynamic farthest-neighbor data structures.

☆ The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Guneykan Ozgul
Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $ρ=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $κ_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $κ_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $Ω(ρ^4/\logρ)$ classical queries but only $Θ(ρ)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.

Given a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices, random $k$-out sampling forms a spanning subgraph by having each vertex independently choose $k$ incident edges uniformly with replacement. We prove that, for every integer $k\geq2$, the expected number of original edges joining distinct sampled components is $O(n/k)$. This resolves the conjecture of Holm, King, Thorup, Zamir, and Zwick in its full range, improving their logarithmic sampling requirement to the optimal threshold of two choices per vertex. The bound fails for $k=1$, and the dependence $O(n/k)$ is tight up to constant factors. Our result holds with replacement and consequently also without replacement. In particular, this implies that contracting just two independent local choices per vertex suffices to reduce an arbitrary simple graph to a quotient with $O(n)$ edges in expectation, which is crucial in reducing the instance size for many contraction-based algorithms. Our proof uses switching arguments to relate intercomponent edges to bridges and a degree-weighted component potential, whose expectation we also bound with a switching argument.
☆ Optimal Online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation

In the online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation Problem (WCAP), we are given a $k$-edge-connected graph on $n$ vertices and a set of additional edges, called links, with nonnegative costs. Pairs of vertices arrive one by one, and an online algorithm must immediately and irrevocably buy links so that each pair becomes $(k+1)$-edge-connected. The goal is to minimize the total cost of the purchased links. We obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for WCAP, improving the previous $O(\log^2 n)$ bound (SODA 2026). Our bound is asymptotically optimal, even for randomized algorithms in the random-order model. The general problem reduces to the case where the underlying graph is a cycle, for which link costs in $\{0,1\}$ already yield an $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound. Surprisingly, for unit costs on a cycle, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $4$-competitive algorithm, improving the previous $O(\log n)$ bound (SODA 2026), and prove that this ratio is optimal among deterministic algorithms. Thus, with unit costs, cycles are easier than trees, where the optimal competitive ratio is $Θ(\log n)$.

☆ 3SUM Made Simpler (Without Matrix Multiplication), $k$-SUM Hypothesis Refuted for Odd $k$, and Real 3SUM/APSP Derandomized

Recently, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem and a truly subcubic algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem were found by Anthropic, as reported by Alman and Vassilevska Williams (2026). These algorithms relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries, which was obtained by modifying known matrix multiplication techniques of Schönhage (1981) and Coppersmith (1982). 1. We present a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs. It completely avoids the use of matrix multiplication but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion--exclusion (and does not even require fast Fourier transform), and so is conceptually easier to understand (the whole solution is about 5 pages long). 2. Following a similar approach, we obtain a randomized algorithm for $k$-SUM for integer inputs for odd constant $k$ in $O(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil-\varepsilon_k})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon_k>0$, disproving the $k$-SUM Hypothesis for all odd $k$. 3. Existing reductions from 3SUM and APSP to selected-entries rectangular matrix multiplication were randomized in the case of real-valued input. We present new deterministic reductions, yielding a truly subquadratic deterministic algorithm for Real 3SUM and a truly subcubic deterministic algorithm for Real APSP.
☆ The C-3PO Framework: Algorithms for $\#\mathrm{BIS}$-Hard Problems on Graphs with Low Threshold Rank or High Girth

We give approximate counting and sampling algorithms for spin models on graphs of low threshold rank or high girth. Given any $n$-vertex graph $G$, let $k_η= k_η(G)$ count normalized-Laplacian eigenvalues strictly below $η$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-approximate counting algorithm outputs an estimate $\widehat Z$ of the partition function $Z$ satisfying $(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z$ with probability at least $3/4$. An $\varepsilon$-approximate sampling algorithm outputs a configuration whose distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the target distribution. We give the following results: (a) Ferromagnetic Potts. Fix $q\ge2$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $β_0(q,η)$ such that, for every inverse temperature $β\geβ_0$, the zero-field $q$-state Potts model admits approximate counting and sampling algorithms: (i) On arbitrary graphs in time $\exp(O(k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) Fix $Δ\ge 3$. On $Δ$-regular graphs of girth $g$ in time $\exp(O(n e^{-g})) \operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (b) Bipartite hard-core. Fix $Δ\ge3$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $λ_0(Δ,η)$ such that, for every fugacity $λ\geλ_0$, the hard-core model admits approximate counting and sampling: (i) On $Δ$-regular vertex-transitive bipartite graphs in time $\exp(O (k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) On $Δ$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $g$ in $\exp(O(n e^{- g}))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ All four results follow from verifying the hypotheses of a new framework we call C-3PO. At a high level, the C-3PO algorithm proceeds by enumerating small cuts and reconstructing the original measure through cluster expansions. Underlying the algorithm is an improvement of subspace enumeration methods via active regression.
☆ Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion

We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound. We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.
☆ Revisiting the directed pathwidth of h-semicomplete digraphs

In semicomplete digraphs, $k$-triples are obstructions to bounded directed pathwidth with many algorithmic applications: Fradkin and Seymour [JCTB 2013] showed that a large triple contains a subdivision of every small digraph, and triples were used for irrelevant vertex arguments in routing problems by Fomin and Pilipczuk [JCTB 2019] and Gomes, Lopes, and Sau [ICALP 2025]. Fradkin and Seymour also showed that there is a function $f(k)$ such that every semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth at least $f(k)$ contains a $k$-triple, and their proof gives $f(k)$ triply exponential in $k$. We improve the bound on $f(k)$ to a single exponential and extend the result to $h$-semicomplete digraphs: we show that every $h$-semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth greater than $(h+1) \cdot k \cdot 2^{27k+9}$ contains a $k$-triple, which we find in polynomial time, and no bound subexponential in $k$ or sublinear in $h$ is possible. We also extend the approximation algorithm for directed pathwidth of Fomin and Pilipczuk to $h$-semicomplete digraphs, so its certificates of large directed pathwidth remain valid. Our proof is much shorter than the analysis of Kitsunai et al., and while their algorithm is exact, ours runs in polynomial time. As an application, we show that Arc-Disjoint Paths on $h$-semicomplete digraphs is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by the number of paths and $h$, generalizing the semicomplete case. Finally, unlike in semicomplete digraphs, directed pathwidth does not bound directed cliquewidth: for every $k$, some acyclic $1$-semicomplete digraph, so of directed pathwidth zero, has directed cliquewidth at least $k$.

The classic scheduling problem of minimizing the total weight of tardy jobs ($P_m||\sum_jw_jU_j$) asks for a schedule of jobs each with a processing time, weight, and due date on a constant number of parallel identical machines. A job is late in a schedule if it completes after its due date, and an optimal schedule is one where the total weight of all late jobs is minimized. The classic dynamic programming algorithm of Lawler and Moore [Manag. Sci., 1969] solves this problem in $O(nd_{\max}^m)$ where $n$ is the number of jobs, $d_{\max}$ is the maximum due date of any job, and $m$ is the number of identical machines. We show that it is sufficient to only compute part of the dynamic program and obtain the running time $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^{m + 1})$ where $\tilde{O}$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This affirmatively answers the open question posed by Hermelin, Molter, and Shabtay [INFORMS J. Comput., 2024], whether a running time of $\tilde{O}(n + d_{\max}^2)$ is possible on a single machine.
☆ Degree Realization with Maximum Matching
Amotz Bar-Noy, Igor Kalinichev, David Peleg, Dror Rawitz

We present a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. The decision version of this problem requires to determine whether a sequence $d$ admits a realization with a matching of size $ν$ (without computing such a realization). Recently, it was shown that it can be done by verifying a series of inequalities. We improve the existing characterization by reducing the number of inequalities.

☆ A Better Lower Bound for Sublinear Metric Steiner Tree
Sepideh Mahabadi, Jakub Tarnawski, Ali Vakilian
In the metric Steiner tree problem, we are given an $n$-point metric space $(V,w)$ and a set of terminals $T\subseteq V$, and we are interested in the smallest total weight $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ of a tree that contains every terminal and may also use points of $V\setminus T$. We work in the distance-oracle model: the algorithm knows $V$ and $T$ in advance and learns $w$ only by querying a single entry $w(u,v)$ at a time. The goal is to estimate $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ with the minimum number of queries. A factor of $2$ is achievable with nearly linear number of queries, so the interesting question is the query complexity of algorithms with an approximation ratio strictly below $2$. We prove that for every fixed $η\in(0,1)$, every randomized $(2-η)$-approximation algorithm must make more than $\widetildeΩ(n^{7/5})$ queries, improving upon the previously known bound of $\widetildeΩ(n^{6/5})$. Given that the best known upper bound shows that $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$ queries suffice, the exponent of this problem now lies between $7/5$ and $5/3$, up to logarithmic factors.

For the bound in the number $m$ of clauses, at clause density one, the crossover point drops to about $2^{420}$ clauses from $2^{33858}$; for general 3-SAT, in the number $n$ of variables, our estimate drops to $2^{8.6\cdot10^9}$ variables from $2^{2.2\cdot10^{12}}$. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$.
